prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- China has refused nine U.S. Navy ships and one Air Force jet entry to Hong Kong in the past month, U.S. military officials said Friday. China has refused the USS Reuben James, seen in a 1989 photo, a Christmas port call in Hong Kong. Senior Navy officials said that Beijing denied permission for the USS Reuben James, a Navy frigate, to make a holiday port call for sailors at the end of December. The rejection occurred last week, at the same time China refused to allow the USS Kitty Hawk aircraft carrier battle group into Hong Kong for a Thanksgiving holiday port call. A U.S. Air Force C-17 flight that had been scheduled for a routine resupply of the U.S. Consulate in Hong Kong also was denied permission to enter, Navy officials said. The Kitty Hawk battle group was eventually granted permission to enter, but by then the ships were well on their way to port in Japan. Days earlier, China refused to give two U.S. Navy minesweepers safe harbor in Hong Kong during a storm on the high seas. The United States has filed a formal protest with China over the decisions. U.S. officials are baffled about the reason or reasons for the port call refusals. China recently has expressed concerns about U.S. arms sales to Taiwan and President Bush's October presentation of a Congressional Gold Medal to the Dalai Lama, the exiled Tibetan spiritual leader.  Watch China put the blame on the U.S. » . There is speculation that the Chinese may have been conducting military exercises that they didn't want the U.S. Navy to see. Others think the refusals may have been the result of a misunderstanding. Officials could not explain why the rejection of the Reuben James had not been disclosed before, even though reporters had repeatedly asked if there were any other pending port calls. One senior Navy official expressed dismay that the information had not been made public by the Pentagon. White House deputy spokesman Scott Stanzel told reporters the White House is "aware" of the latest refusals and referred reporters to the Pentagon. Stanzel said a "clarification" on the matter was being sought from Beijing. White House and other Bush administration officials have sought to defuse tensions with China, saying the United States wants to move ahead on broader issues of military cooperation. Navy officials, meanwhile, say Japan is tightening approvals for Chinese navy visits into its ports. Crew members from a Chinese ship making a port call in Japan may not be allowed to tour a Japanese Aegis warship. The U.S.-designed Aegis weapons system enables coordinated operations against threats from aircraft and missiles, surface ships and submarines. It is not clear if the Japanese decision was made at the request of the United States. E-mail to a friend .

outputs.L1:
WASHINGTON (CNN) — China has denied entry to Hong Kong for nine U.S. Navy ships and one Air Force jet over the past month, U.S. military officials said Friday.

Senior Navy officials said Beijing had refused permission for the USS *Reuben James*, a Navy frigate shown in a 1989 photograph, to make a holiday port call for sailors at the end of December. The rejection came last week, at the same time China denied the USS *Kitty Hawk* aircraft carrier battle group entry to Hong Kong for a Thanksgiving port call.

A U.S. Air Force C-17 flight scheduled to conduct a routine resupply mission for the U.S. Consulate in Hong Kong was also denied permission to enter, Navy officials said.

The *Kitty Hawk* battle group was eventually granted permission to enter, but by then the ships were already well on their way to port in Japan. Days earlier, China had refused to provide safe harbor in Hong Kong to two U.S. Navy minesweepers during a storm on the high seas.

The United States has filed a formal protest with China over the decisions. U.S. officials remain baffled by the reason—or reasons—for the port-call refusals.

China has recently expressed concern over U.S. arms sales to Taiwan and President Bush’s presentation in October of a Congressional Gold Medal to the Dalai Lama, Tibet’s exiled spiritual leader. Watch China place the blame on the United States »

There is speculation that China may have been conducting military exercises it did not want the U.S. Navy to observe. Others believe the refusals may have resulted from a misunderstanding.

Officials could not explain why the rejection of the *Reuben James* had not been disclosed earlier, despite reporters’ repeated questions about whether any other port calls were pending. One senior Navy official expressed dismay that the Pentagon had not made the information public.

White House Deputy Press Secretary Scott Stanzel told reporters that the White House was “aware” of the latest refusals and referred further questions to the Pentagon. Stanzel said the administration was seeking “clarification” from Beijing.

White House officials and other members of the Bush administration have sought to ease tensions with China, saying the United States wants to move forward on broader issues of military cooperation.

Meanwhile, Navy officials said Japan is tightening its approval process for Chinese naval visits to Japanese ports. Crew members from a Chinese ship making a port call in Japan may not be permitted to tour a Japanese Aegis warship.

The U.S.-designed Aegis weapons system enables coordinated operations against threats posed by aircraft and missiles, surface ships, and submarines. It remains unclear whether Japan’s decision was made at the request of the United States.

outputs.L2:
WASHINGTON (CNN) — U.S. military officials said Friday that, during the previous month, China had blocked nine American naval vessels and one Air Force aircraft from entering Hong Kong.

Among those denied access was the USS Reuben James, a Navy frigate pictured in a 1989 photograph. Senior Navy officials said Beijing last week rejected a request for the ship to make a Christmas visit at the end of December, which would have provided shore leave for its sailors.

That decision came as China also turned away the USS Kitty Hawk aircraft-carrier battle group, which had planned to spend the Thanksgiving holiday in Hong Kong. Although Beijing later approved the group’s entry, the vessels were already far along on their journey to a Japanese port.

Navy officials also reported that Chinese authorities refused entry to a U.S. Air Force C-17 scheduled to carry out a routine resupply mission for the American Consulate in Hong Kong.

Several days before the Kitty Hawk incident, China had declined to provide safe harbor in Hong Kong to two U.S. Navy minesweepers caught in a storm at sea.

Washington lodged an official protest with Beijing over the series of decisions. American officials said they remained puzzled about China’s motives.

Possible explanations include recent Chinese objections to U.S. weapons sales to Taiwan and President Bush’s presentation of the Congressional Gold Medal in October to the Dalai Lama, Tibet’s exiled spiritual leader. Some have also suggested that China may have been holding military exercises it did not want the U.S. Navy to observe. Others believe the denials could have resulted from a misunderstanding. China, meanwhile, placed responsibility on the United States.

Officials could not say why the Reuben James denial had not been revealed earlier, despite repeated questions from reporters about whether other port visits were awaiting approval. One senior Navy official voiced frustration that the Pentagon had failed to disclose the information.

Deputy White House spokesman Scott Stanzel said the administration was aware of the additional refusals but directed questions to the Pentagon. He added that Washington was asking Beijing to clarify the situation.

Officials at the White House and elsewhere in the Bush administration attempted to ease friction with China, emphasizing that the United States wanted to continue pursuing wider military cooperation.

At the same time, Navy officials said Japan was imposing stricter approval requirements for Chinese naval visits to Japanese ports. Sailors from a Chinese vessel visiting Japan might also be prohibited from touring a Japanese Aegis warship.

Designed in the United States, the Aegis weapons system allows forces to coordinate responses to dangers posed by aircraft, missiles, surface vessels, and submarines. It remained uncertain whether Japan’s decision had been made at Washington’s request.
outputs.L3:
Within the span of a month, China refused permission for nine U.S. Navy ships and one U.S. Air Force aircraft to enter Hong Kong. The rejected requests included planned holiday port calls by the USS *Reuben James* and the USS *Kitty Hawk* carrier battle group. Although China later granted permission for the *Kitty Hawk* group to visit, the ships had already departed for Japan.

Chinese authorities also blocked a routine U.S. Consulate resupply flight and denied safe harbor to two Navy minesweepers seeking shelter from a storm. The series of refusals prompted the United States to file a formal diplomatic protest. American officials said they had not received a clear explanation for China’s decisions.

Several possible motives were suggested. The refusals may have reflected Chinese anger over U.S. arms sales to Taiwan or President George W. Bush’s decision to honor the Dalai Lama. Other explanations included undisclosed Chinese military exercises in the region or a simple misunderstanding between the two governments. Without an official explanation from Beijing, however, the reason remained uncertain.
outputs.L4:
China denied entry to Hong Kong to nine U.S. Navy ships and a U.S. Air Force resupply aircraft over the course of roughly a month, leading Washington to lodge a formal diplomatic protest and seek an explanation from Beijing. U.S. officials said the number and timing of the refusals suggested more than an isolated scheduling or paperwork problem, although China did not provide a consistent public reason for its decisions.

The most prominent incident involved the aircraft carrier USS *Kitty Hawk* and its accompanying strike group, which had planned a Thanksgiving port call in Hong Kong. Thousands of sailors and their family members had arranged to spend the holiday together there, but Chinese authorities withheld permission for the visit. Beijing later indicated that the ships could enter on humanitarian grounds, but by then the group had already turned away and was too far from Hong Kong to return as scheduled.

Other refusals involved U.S. vessels seeking routine port access, including Navy minesweepers that requested shelter from severe weather. Chinese authorities also denied clearance to an Air Force cargo aircraft assigned to support the U.S. consulate in Hong Kong. Taken together, the incidents affected nine naval vessels and one military aircraft, making the pattern unusually broad.

American officials asked whether the denials were politically motivated, linked to military activity China did not want observed, or simply the result of administrative confusion. Among the possible political explanations were Beijing’s anger over U.S. arms sales to Taiwan and President George W. Bush’s meeting with the Dalai Lama, whom China accused of promoting Tibetan separatism. Some U.S. officials also considered whether China had been conducting military exercises near Hong Kong and wanted to limit the presence of American ships and aircraft.

The United States emphasized that routine military visits to Hong Kong had long served as a practical channel of contact between the two countries. Officials warned that denying even storm shelter raised concerns beyond diplomatic protocol because it could endanger sailors and ships at sea. The repeated refusals therefore added strain to an already sensitive U.S.-China relationship and increased doubts in Washington about the reliability and transparency of Beijing’s military decision-making.
